provenance.source: NCERT Mathematics Class 8, Chapter 2 'Linear Equations in One Variable'. The misconceptions are the ones this topic reliably produces at the point where arithmetic becomes algebra: reading an equation as an instruction to compute rather than as a statement of balance, and losing the sign when a term crosses the equals.
provenance.note: m1 is the deepest one in the chapter and it is not a slip. In arithmetic '=' has always meant 'now write the answer'. Reading it as 'these two sides are the same thing' is a genuinely new idea, and a student who does not make that switch will pass Class 8 by pattern-matching and fall over in Class 9. concepts.title: An equation is a balance, not an instruction
concepts.statement: An equation means this: the things on both sides of the equal sign are the same. $2x + 3 = 11$ means ‘the number which, when multiplied by 2 and then 3 is added, gives 11’. In a linear equation, the highest power of the variable is 1.
concepts.hook: Think of a weighing balance. On one pan there are 2 mangoes and a 300 gram weight, and on the other there is a 1100 gram weight. The balance is level. Now tell me, how much is one mango? What you just thought is exactly solving an equation. The question is: if I put 100 gram more on one pan, what must I do so that the balance stays level?

analogies.text: Weighing balance: whatever you do on one side, you must do the same on the other side, otherwise it will not stay equal.
Two friends have equal money. If one is given ₹50, the other must also be given ₹50. Only then will they stay equal.

formulas.note: The general form of a linear equation. The power of x is 1.
Left Hand Side and Right Hand Side — both are equal. That is the whole game.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: $=$ means ‘now write the answer’. In $2x + 3 = 11$, the answer is 11.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In arithmetic, after $5 + 3 = $ the answer always came, so this habit formed. But in an equation, $=$ says that both sides are the same — it is a statement, not an order. 11 is not the answer; it is already written. What we have to find is $x$.
misconceptions.correction: $=$ means ‘both sides are equal’. The answer is the value which, when put in place of $x$, makes both sides equal.
misconceptions.probe: In $2x + 3 = 11$, what do we have to find — $x$ or 11? And put $x = 4$ and check: did both sides become equal?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: If you do something on one side, there is no need to do it on the other side.
misconceptions.why_wrong: If you make one pan of the balance lighter, it will tilt. In an equation also, if you remove 3 from one side and not from the other, the equality breaks — and what you get will be a wrong answer.
misconceptions.correction: Whatever you do on one side, do exactly the same on the other side too. Every time.
misconceptions.probe: In $2x + 3 = 11$, if you remove 3 only from the left, the left becomes $2x$. Now what will the right side remain — 11 or 8? Why?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When you take a term to the other side, the sign stays the same. From $2x + 3 = 11$ to $2x = 11 + 3$.
misconceptions.why_wrong: ‘Taking it to the other side’ is actually subtracting from both sides. To remove $+3$, we subtract 3 from both sides, so the other side becomes $-3$. The sign changes because the opposite operation is being done.
misconceptions.correction: When it crosses to the other side, plus becomes minus and minus becomes plus. Multiplication becomes division.
misconceptions.probe: $2x + 3 = 11$. Subtract 3 from both sides and write what is left. Now tell me, did the right side become 14 or 8?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: $x^2 + 3 = 7$ is also a linear equation, because it has only one variable.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Linear means the power of the variable is 1. In $x^2$, the power is 2, so it is quadratic. Having one variable is not enough — we must look at the power.
misconceptions.correction: Linear = the highest power of the variable is 1. $x$ is okay, $x^2$ is not, and $\frac{1}{x}$ is also not.
misconceptions.probe: In $x^2 + 3 = 7$, what is the power of $x$? And what should it be for it to be linear?

steps: Check: put $x = 4$, then LHS is $= 2 \times 4 + 3 = 11$, and RHS is $= 11$. Equal.
Bring the variable to one side — subtract $3x$ from both sides: $5x - 3x - 7 = 5$

questions.stem: In $2x + 3 = 11$, what do we have to find?

options.text: There is nothing to find; it is already solved

questions.solution: The equation says that both sides are equal. 11 is already known; we have to find $x$ — the number which, when put there, makes both sides equal. Here, $x = 4$.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a linear equation?
questions.solution: Linear means the highest power of the variable is 1. In $x^2$, the power is 2, so it is quadratic. In the other three, the power of $x$ is 1 — $\frac{x}{2}$ is also just $\frac{1}{2}x$.

questions.stem: To remove 3 from $2x + 3 = 11$, what should we do?

options.text: Take 3 to the right as it is — $2x = 11 + 3$

questions.solution: To keep the balance equal, whatever we subtract from the left must also be subtracted from the right: $2x + 3 - 3 = 11 - 3$, that is $2x = 8$. That is why the sign changes when it ‘crosses over’ — actually, it is subtraction.

questions.stem: Solve $2x + 3 = 11$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Subtract 3 from both sides: $2x = 8$. Divide both sides by 2: $x = 4$. Check: $2 \times 4 + 3 = 11$ ✓

questions.stem: Solve $5x - 7 = 3x + 5$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Subtract $3x$ from both sides: $2x - 7 = 5$. Add 7 to both sides: $2x = 12$. Divide: $x = 6$. Check: LHS $= 23$, RHS $= 23$ ✓

questions.stem: Rahul wrote: ‘$3x - 5 = 10$, so $3x = 10 - 5 = 5$, so $x = \frac{5}{3}$.’ Where is the mistake?

options.text: When $-5$ crosses over, it becomes $+5$, so $3x = 15$ and $x = 5$
He should not have divided by 3

questions.solution: To remove $-5$, we have to ADD 5 to both sides: $3x - 5 + 5 = 10 + 5$, that is $3x = 15$ and $x = 5$. Rahul subtracted it. A check would catch it at once: $3 \times \frac{5}{3} - 5 = 0$, not 10.

questions.stem: When we put $x = 4$, what do we get on both sides of $3x - 2 = 10$?

options.text: LHS $= 10$, RHS $= 10$ — equal, so $x = 4$ is correct
There is no point in putting it and checking

questions.solution: LHS $= 3 \times 4 - 2 = 12 - 2 = 10$. RHS $= 10$. Both are equal, so $x = 4$ is correct. The answer to every equation can be checked like this by yourself — this habit saves the most marks in the exam.

questions.stem: Solve $4(x - 2) = 2x + 6$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: First open the bracket (distributive law): $4x - 8 = 2x + 6$. Subtract $2x$ from both sides: $2x - 8 = 6$. Add 8 to both sides: $2x = 14$. Divide: $x = 7$. Check: LHS $= 4(7-2) = 20$, RHS $= 2 \times 7 + 6 = 20$ ✓

questions.stem: A friend says: ‘After solving an equation, why should we check? It only wastes time.’ Explain to him why checking is important, and give one example.

rubric: Equation ka matlab hi dono taraf barabar hona hai, to check karna hi asli sabooth hai
Sign ki galti (jaise minus paar jaate waqt) solve karte waqt dikhti nahi, check karte waqt turant dikhti hai
Ek thos udaharan diya jahan galat jawab check me pakda gaya
Check me sirf kuch second lagte hain aur poora number bach jaata hai

questions.solution: An equation itself says that both sides are equal — so putting the answer and checking is not extra work, it is the real proof. And while solving, the most common mistake is with the sign, which does not show by itself. For example, in $3x - 5 = 10$, someone may write $3x = 5$ and get $x = \frac{5}{3}$ — it looks okay. But put it and check: $3 \times \frac{5}{3} - 5 = 0$, and it should have been 10. The mistake is caught at once. Checking takes ten seconds and saves the marks for the whole question.
